newsitem.title: FRANCE: Supreme Court won't close French sleaze probes.
newsitem.headline: Supreme Court won't close French sleaze probes.

text.p: The French Supreme Court refused on Thursday to set a legal precedent which could have closed dozens of corruption investigations against politicians and senior businessmen.
The court threw out appeals by three public figures convicted of receiving the proceeds of misuse of corporate funds who had argued that the offences were covered by the statute of limitations.

Former Lyon mayor Michel Noir, Cannes mayor Michel Mouillot and star television newscaster Patrick Poivre d'Arvor, convicted on matters dating back to the 1980s, had argued they could only be prosecuted within three years of the offence being committed.
The Supreme Court ruled they were liable to prosecution up to three years after the offence was discovered and upheld their convictions.

A Lyon court gave Noir and Mouillot 18-month suspended jail terms and hefty fines a year ago for their roles in an illicit campaign funding scheme. Poivre d'Arvor got a 15-month suspended term for accepting lavish gifts including Caribbean holidays.

Money and gifts came from corporate funds embezzled by Noir's businessman son-in-law Pierre Botton. Botton, serving a three-and-a-half year jail sentence, has not appealed and recently tried to commit suicide in prison after being denied parole.

Justice sources said several investigating magistrates had been awaiting the Supreme Court's ruling to pursue their own probes. A host of investigations target the ruling centre-right coalition parties as well as the opposition Socialists and Communists.

The government plans to limit the definition of misuse of corporate funds and the statute of limitations applying to such offences, which carry a maximum five-year jail sentence and fines of up to 2.5 million francs ($500,000).
Noir, Mouillot and Poivre d'Arvor had appealed to the Supreme Court on technicalities. The court could not modify the sentences but could either confirm them or order a retrial.

Because the sentences were confirmed, Noir, a member of parliament and a former trade minister once tipped as a possible presidential candidate, and Mouillot became ineligible for public office for five years.

Noir, who recently starred in a play in a Lyon theatre, said later he was quitting politics for good. "The Supreme Court has ruled. I am stopping my work as a deputy today. My political life is now finished," he said in a statement.

In a separate case, Noir is appealing against a 12-month suspended sentence for diverting eight million francs ($1.6 million) of Lyon's municipal funds to finance political campaigns and personal expenses.

Mouillot is in prison, awaiting trial in yet another case on accusations that he extorted money from casinos in his Riviera resort. The local council has two weeks from the time it is officially notified of the Court ruling to elect a new mayor. But Mouillot may resign before then.
